A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same kernel-regression work. Their text, equations, figures, and complete appendices support comparison. The shared theoretical material can be matched reliably despite pagination changes and the addition of Appendix D.

before.justification: Section 4.3 and Figure 2 report original numerical comparisons of uncertainty-region areas, averaged over 1,000 randomly generated latent functions.

after.justification: The original numerical comparison is retained. Section 4.3 and Figure 3 additionally report original safe-control feasibility and computation-time results.

M1.justification: The kernel bound and its scalar optimization remain unchanged. Section 4.3 and Appendix D add a control adaptation that jointly optimizes the control input and noise parameter, uses penalized safety-constraint slack, and includes a ten-nearest-neighbor implementation.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates synthetic function-estimation uncertainty on [0,4]. v2 retains this coverage and adds safe control for an uncertain scalar nonlinear system on [-2,2], extending evaluation from estimation accuracy to finding feasible control inputs.

E2.justification: Figure 2 retains the optimal bound, fixed-sigma relaxation, and Abbasi-Yadkori probabilistic bound referenced through Fiedler et al. (2024). The new control comparison adds a ten-nearest-neighbor variant alongside the full-data implementations; the external probabilistic comparator is reused.

E3.justification: The original uncertainty-area evaluation retains its settings. The new control evaluation introduces a grid of 500 test states, bounded control inputs, feasible-problem percentage and solve-time metrics, and a feasibility criterion based on optimal slack being at most 10^-6.

E4.justification: Figure 3 adds a targeted comparison of full-data bounds against bounds using the ten nearest training points. This tests the effect of local data selection on control feasibility and computation time; no comparable subset-selection analysis appears in v1.

E5.justification: v2 reports 20 repetitions with random noise realizations for the new control experiment. Both versions retain the original 1,000-run comparison and 5th/95th-percentile shading; Figure 3 uses the same percentile convention. This is additional repetition information, not a reduction in the original experiment's runs.

E6.justification: Figures 1 and 2 retain their results. New Figure 3 reports control feasibility and runtime curves: the full-data proposed bound provides higher feasibility at greater computational cost, while its nearest-neighbor variant achieves success rates similar to the probabilistic bound with lower solve times.

T1.justification: The principal assumptions, theorem, propositions, and derivations are retained. Section 4.1 changes the noise-free specialization from Gamma_w squared equal to zero to a limiting statement. Appendix C's revised footnote explicitly allows zero multipliers in the case analysis, refining its treatment of overlapping active sets.

C1.justification: The abstract and central claim of tight kernel-regression bounds remain stable. The conclusion newly claims demonstrated safe-control utility and rigorous certification of subset-of-data or mixture-of-experts strategies for large datasets, extending the stated practical contributions.

C2.justification: v1 identifies large-data computation and conditioning as its most critical unresolved limitation. v2 reframes scalability around certified subset selection and interprets the control feasibility/runtime tradeoff, while warning about probabilistic guarantees under test-dependent subsets. Section 4.4 also adds substantive claims about compensating kernel misspecification and detecting underestimated norm bounds.

D1.justification: v2 adds reproduction-code and archival links, plus Appendix D's optimization formulation, CasADi/IPOPT implementation, hardware, and parameter table, including gamma = 0.95 and slack penalty 10^4. Conversely, v1's original comparison disclosure of 14-core parallel execution and approximately 18 hours total runtime is removed.

R1.justification: v2 adds references supporting control-barrier applications, implementation software, kernel-basis transformations, and norm/kernel estimation, including Agrawal and Sreenath, Ames et al., and Jagtap et al. Its positioning against existing kernel bounds remains substantially unchanged. The Kanagawa citation is updated to the later treatment of the same connections.

P1.justification: v2 locally rewrites the contribution statement and explanations, separates limitations into Section 4.4, revises the conclusion, and adds Appendix D. Most of the introduction, method exposition, and proofs retain their wording and order.

P2.justification: v2 adds the two-panel control-results Figure 3 and implementation-parameter Table 1. Figure 1 is unchanged; Figure 2 retains its plotted results but changes its vertical-axis wording from confidence region to uncertainty region. Appendix sections also receive new page breaks.

improvement.justification: v2 strengthens v1's suggested downstream utility with explicit control feasibility/runtime evidence and supplies useful implementation details and code-access links. These improve practical substantiation while retaining the core theory. The gain remains limited by the single synthetic control example, the broader mixture-of-experts claim lacking direct evaluation, and removal of the original experiment's runtime disclosure.
